questions.stem: A 45-year-old healthcare worker received a needlestick injury. The recipient was known to be a hepatitis B vaccine non-responder despite two vaccination courses. Recipient: HBsAg negative Hepatitis B surface antibody 2 mIU/mL HBV cAb negative Source: HBsAg positive, HBeAg positive, HBeAb negative HBV DNA 62 million U/mL
questions.lead_in: What is the most appropriate treatment?

options.text: A single dose of hepatitis B vaccine
An accelerated course of hepatitis B vaccination
Single dose of HBIG and an accelerated course of hepatitis B vaccine
Two doses of hepatitis B immunoglobulin (HBIG) 1 month apart

questions.explanation: Two doses of hepatitis B immunoglobulin (HBIG) 1 month apart The healthcare worker has no immunity to hepatitis B and has sustained a significant exposure to a patient who is HBsAg+ and thus requires immediate intervention. The CDC recommend that nonresponders should preferably receive two doses of HBIG 1 month apart as postexposure prophylaxis. Adequate protection against infection would not be provided by the alternative options. If the recipient’s anti-HBsAb status is unknown, then the CDC recommend a single dose of HBIG and commencing a course of HBV vaccination.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 1 Q44

questions.stem: A 39-year-old woman was reviewed with a new diagnosis of HIV and hepatitis B co-infection. A pregnancy test was negative. Despite multiple educational meetings she declined HIV treatment but was interested in hepatitis B treatment. Investigations: AST 89 IU/L ALT 98 units/L CD4 count 434 cells/μL HIV viral load 55,000 copies/mL HBsAg positive HBV viral load 540,000 IU/mL Liver biopsy showed significant fibrosis but no cirrhosis
questions.lead_in: What is the most appropriate treatment to offer?
questions.explanation: Peginterferon alfa 2B The patient is refusing HIV treatment at this time. The concern is that using an agent for her hepatitis that also has activity against HIV would lead to the development of HIV resistance. Entecavir, lamivudine, tenofovir, and emtricitabine are all active against both HIV and HBV . Only peginterferon alfa 2B alone will not lead to HIV-resistance. Remember that interferon therapy has many disadvantages, multiple side effects (i.e., influenza-like syndrome, myalgias, depression, fatigue, etc.) and is only given IM. If the patient would have accepted treatment for both HIV and HBV , then combination therapy with tenofovir, emtricitabine, and dolutegravir would have been the optimal choice. This regimen offers three active drugs against HIV as recommended by the DHHS guidelines and at the same time would offer two active drugs against hepatitis B (tenofovir and emtricitabine).
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 3 Q8

questions.stem: A 35-year-old woman presented with a 3-week history of nausea, vomiting, and abdominal pain, and 10 days of jaundice. She was an active IV drug user. On physical exam, she was jaundiced with right upper quadrant tenderness. Investigations: ALT 2000 IU/mL AST 900 IU/mL HAV IgM negative, HAV PCR negative HCV IgG negative, HCV PCR negative HBVsAg positive, anti-HBs negative anti-HBc IgM positive, anti-HBc total positive HBe Ag positive, anti-HBe negative
questions.lead_in: What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Acute hepatitis B Hepatitis C and Hepatitis A testing are both negative. Hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg) is a marker for active replication signifying that the patient is infectious. It is present in high amounts during the acute phase of infection. It can also be present during the chronic phase of infection if the immune system fails to clear the virus effectively. If HBsAg is present at all the patient should be considered contagious. If it is present for 6 months or more the patient is considered to have chronic hepatitis B. Differentiation between chronic replicating and chronic, nonreplicating is the presence of hepatitis B e antigen (HBeAg) and anti-HBe antibodies. In chronic, replicating hepatitis B the patient will be positive for HBeAg; during chronic, nonreplicating infection anti-HBe antibodies will be present. In both chronic conditions the total core antibody (anti-HBc) will be positive while anti-HBc IgM will be negative. If NAAT testing is performed during this time the amount of HBV DNA will be higher during chronic, replicating hepatitis B. This person is in the acute phase of infection as the HBsAg is positive and no antibodies to the surface antigen have been generated. In addition, the total and IgM core (HBc) antibodies are present, as is the case in acute hepatitis B.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 5 Q3

questions.stem: A 35-year-old woman presented with jaundice, vomiting, and right upper quadrant pain. She was 22/40 weeks pregnant. She was sexually active and was not using condoms. She had received a blood transfusion for anemia 2 weeks prior to this admission. She was a nurse at a local physician’s office and had received all recommended vaccinations 5 years ago when she started working. Investigations: ALT 750 IU/L AST 2320 IU/L
questions.lead_in: What is the most likely cause of her hepatitis?
questions.explanation: Herpes simplex virus Both hepatitis B and herpes simplex virus infection can cause a fulminant hepatitis. She is unlikely to get HBV as she is vaccinated. Herpes simplex has been described to more commonly cause fulminant hepatitis in pregnancy. Hepatitis G virus (GBV-C) is transmitted by transfusion but does not cause any known disease. CMV can cause a mild hepatitis, but HSV would more commonly cause fulminant hepatitis.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 6 Q12

questions.stem: A 43-year-old man presented with nausea, anorexia, and right upper quadrant pain. He was known to have coinfection with HIV and hepatitis B. He recently switched his HIV antiretroviral therapy from tenofovir/emtricitabine/ efavirenz to abacavir/lamivudine and raltegravir due to concerns over worsening renal function. He was sexually active and reported 4 casual male partners in the last 6 months, without using condoms. He had not traveled outside of the United States and had never used recreational intravenous drugs. On physical exam, he had scleral icterus and tender hepatomegaly of 3 cm. Investigations: CD4 count 520 cells/μL HIV viral load <20 copies/mL AST 1623 U/L ALT 824 U/L Total bilirubin 4.2 mg/dL (0.1–1.2) Hepatitis C IgG negative Hepatitis B surface antigen positive Hepatitis B core IgM positive HLAB5701 negative Right upper quadrant sonogram demonstrated no gallstones or biliary duct dilation.
questions.lead_in: What is the most likely etiology?
questions.explanation: Hepatitis B virus flare In this patient with HIV–HBV co-infection, the most likely cause of the acute hepatitis is a flare of the chronic hepatitis B precipitated by the change from a tenofovir-based ART to one containing lamivudine. Monotherapy with lamivudine for HBV is not recommended due to the risk of drug resistance and an acute flare in HBV . This is also supported by the positive HBV core IgM which often is seen in flares. Drug-induced liver injury from the current ART is less likely and fails to explain the hepatitis B virus serologies. Hepatitis D virus is most closely associated with IVDA or travel to areas of endemicity such as the Mediterranean basin. HIV cholangiopathy and MAC are primarily seen in patients with advanced AIDS and CD4 <50–100.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 8 Q23

questions.stem: A 27-year-old man presented with confusion. He had been discharged 3 days earlier after recovering from an episode of acute hepatitis and jaundice. He was an active intravenous drug user. Investigations: Day 1 Day 7 Day 10 AST (IU/L) 1200 – 2200 ALT (IU/L) 1500 180 3000 INR 1.2 – 3.5 Total bilirubin (mg/dL) 0.9 – 5.4 Serology HAV IgM negative HBV sAg positive HBV cAb IgM positive HCV Ab negative HBV sAg positive HBV DNA positive HCV RNA negative HIV Ag/Ab negative
questions.lead_in: What is the most likely explanation?

options.text: Acute HCV superimposed on chronic HBV

questions.explanation: Co-infection with HBV and HDV The timing is most consistent with co-infection with HBV and HDV , which is more likely to present with worsening liver disease. The serologies are not consistent with acute infection with either HAV or HCV but are consistent with acute HBV infection, which initially improved. Acute HIV infection does not cause a fulminant hepatitis, although it can raise transaminases.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 3 Q25

questions.stem: A 47-year-old man was being treated for hepatitis C with ledipasvir/sofosbuvir. Investigations: HAV IgG positive HBV cAb positive, HBV sAg negative, HBV sAb 0 HBV DNA undetectable A B HCV IgG positive, HCV genotype 1a Liver biopsy showed grade 1 inflammation and stage 3 fibrosis with features of both chronic HCV and nonalcoholic steatohepatitis. Baseline Week 4 Week 11 ALT (IU/L) 170 35 2250 AST (IU/L) 289 32 2970 HCV viral load (IU/mL) 1,200,000 Undetectable Undetectable INR 1.8 Total bilirubin (mg/dL) 7.2
questions.lead_in: What is the most likely reason for the worsening transaminases?
questions.explanation: Reactivation of HBV Reactivation of HBV in a patient with co-infection with HBV and HCV has been reported in patients being treated for HCV . A patient responding to HCV treatment who has a flare of hepatitis, but still with undetectable HCV viral loads, should be evaluated for HBV . Drug reaction is possible but rarely causes transaminases this elevated. For more information, see https://www.hhs.gov/hepatitis/blog/2017/1/17/hbv-reactivation-during-hcv-treatmen t.html
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 4 Q25

questions.question: Hepatitis B core Ab positive only

parts.text: A.  Three explanations other than false positives
B.  What two tests of interventions will help you sort is out?

cohort_answer.text:
Resolved acute infection; Occult infection (surface ag/ab has disappeared or hasn't appeared yet); Resolving acute infection
Hep B DNA (viral load for chronicity), Hep Bc IgM (acute infx). If both negative, false pos. If both pos, acute infx

questions.question: 2. HIV infected patient with HIV that has K103N mutation in treatment naive patient on PPI and with chronic hepB and prior MI.

parts.text: A. What is appropriate initial regimen?
B.  Name two initial drugs not appropriate for this patient and justify.
C. What three non infectious issues must be monitored in him?

cohort_answer.text:
K103N mutation = NVP and EFV resistance; PPIs: avoid RVP and ATV/r; MI: avoid abacavir; Chronic Hep B = include 3TC / TDF. DTG/TDF/FTC; RAL/TDF/FTC; RAL/TAF/FTC
K103N mutation = NVP and EFV resistance; PPIs: avoid RVP and ATV/r; MI: avoid abacavir; Dyslipidemia: remember PEE – PI, Elvitegravir, EFV (PEE)
Bone mineral density (TDF); Renal function (TDF); Metabolic risk factors (DTG); Liver enzymes

questions.question: 20.  HepB in pregnancy at fourteen weeks.

parts.text: A.  What treatment?
B.  What test?
C.  When to start?
D. What treatment(s) in baby with timing?

cohort_answer.text:
Tenofovir disoproxil fumarate
If HepBs ag pos, check e ag, if pos then viral load, ALT
If e ag neg and viral load >200,000 IU/ml: start tx 24-32 weeks GA and continue till delivery or 12 weeks post partum; If e ag pos and viral load >20,000, start tx as per non pregnant person
Hep B immunoglobulin within 12 hours of life, initiate Hep B vaccine series (up to 7 days post natal)

questions.question: GP recently vaccinated a patient for HBV. He accidentally sends HBV serologies 2 days after (HBsAg pos, HBsAb neg, HBcAb total and IgM neg).

parts.text: Interpret.

questions.model_answer: Interpretation: HBsAg positive, HBsAb negative, HBcAb (total and IgM) negative - this pattern is NOT consistent with vaccine response (vaccine produces isolated anti-HBs). HBsAg positivity with negative anti-HBc so soon after vaccination most likely represents transient antigenemia from the recombinant HBsAg vaccine itself (can be detected for a few days post-vaccination) rather than true infection; absence of anti-HBc argues strongly against actual HBV infection. Recommend repeat serology in 4-6 weeks to confirm clearance/resolution.

questions.question: 14. You are called about a freshly (1h) born infant from a mother who had no prenatal care. Her tests are positive for HIV and hepatitis B.

parts.text: List 2 measures you can take for the infant to prevent HIV infection
b) List 2 measures you can take for the infant to prevent HBV transmission

cohort_answer.text: HIV prevention: Begin ARV regimen within 6-12 hours after birth. 2-drug ARV prophylaxis with 6 weeks ZDV and 3 doses of NVP, or Empiric HIV therapy using ZDV/3TC/NVP or ZDV/3TC/RAL from birth to age 6 weeks. Do not breastfeed. C/S if results available before delivery + intrapartum ZDV. HBV prevention: HBIG (ideally within 12hr); Hepatitis B vaccine.

questions.question: Patient with anti-HBc + all other serology / antigen tests negative.

parts.text: Give 3 explanations other than false positive test
What 2 ways could you further work up (if repeat testing is positive)

cohort_answer.text:
Explanations: Occult Hep B; Resolved acute HBV infection; Resolving acute infx
Further work up: Test HBV DNA; Check IgM HBc (acute resolving)

questions.question: Congenital HIV and HBV to mother with no prenatal care.

parts.text: How to prevent HIV transmission, list two mechanisms?
What two things are given to prevent HBV transmission?

cohort_answer.text: HIV prevention mechanisms: ART during pregnancy; C-section if viral load is >1000 copies; Intrapartum AZT if >1000 (or consider if 50-999 copies, no need if <50 copies); No breastfeeding; Triple empiric HIV therapy for baby. HBV prevention: Treat mother 28wks onwards; HBIG and Hep B vaccine

questions.question: In the following table, fill out if the virus is RNA/DNA, and whether it is enveloped or not. For each virus, name one antiviral that has activity against it, if any (Mumps is given as an example). Table columns: Virus, RNA or DNA, Enveloped (Yes or No), Antiviral. Viruses listed: Mumps, Measles, Hepatitis B, EBV, Influenza, Zika, Ebola.

parts.text: Fill out the table for RNA/DNA, enveloped status, and antiviral for: Mumps, Measles, Hepatitis B, EBV, Influenza, Zika, Ebola

questions.model_answer: Mumps (example): ssRNA (negative-sense), enveloped; no specific antiviral (supportive care). Measles: ssRNA (negative-sense), enveloped; no specific antiviral (supportive care; ribavirin used off-label in severe cases). Hepatitis B: partially double-stranded DNA, enveloped; antivirals - tenofovir or entecavir. EBV: double-stranded DNA, enveloped; no specific approved antiviral (ganciclovir/valganciclovir used off-label for select EBV-driven disease). Influenza: ssRNA (negative-sense, segmented), enveloped; antivirals - oseltamivir (or zanamivir, baloxavir). Zika: ssRNA (positive-sense), enveloped; no approved antiviral. Ebola: ssRNA (negative-sense), enveloped; antivirals - monoclonal antibody therapies (e.g., ansuvimab, atoltivimab/maftivimab/odesivimab); remdesivir has also been studied.
questions.cites: Mandell pp. 557-559 (general principles); virus-specific data drawn from respective chapters
questions.beyond_mandell: Specific virologic classification and antiviral data for individual viruses beyond general principles chapter.

questions.question: A man has the following serology results: HBsAg negative, HBcAb positive, Anti-HBs Ab negative, Anti-HBc Ab negative, HBeAg negative.

parts.text: What are 3 possibilities aside from false positive?
Name two tests or procedures you could do next.

questions.model_answer: a) Possibilities for isolated anti-HBc positive (3, aside from false positive): (1) Resolved past HBV infection with waned anti-HBs to undetectable levels (window/late convalescent period). (2) Occult HBV infection (low-level HBV DNA present despite negative HBsAg). (3) Remote infection acquired many years prior in an endemic region with subsequent loss of anti-HBs. b) Next tests: (1) HBV DNA (to detect occult infection). (2) Anti-HBc IgM (to assess for recent/acute infection window period) and/or repeat anti-HBs after booster vaccine dose (anamnestic response confirms prior immunity).

questions.question: A person has a hepatitis B core Ab positive only.

parts.text: List 4 reasons for this
What is the next step to differentiating the possibilities

questions.model_answer: a) Reasons for isolated HBcAb positive (4): (1) Window period of acute infection (HBsAg cleared, anti-HBs not yet risen). (2) Remote resolved infection with anti-HBs waned below detection over time. (3) Occult chronic HBV infection (low-level HBsAg below assay detection). (4) False-positive result (low-prevalence population). b) Next step: check HBV DNA and anti-HBc IgM; give a single vaccine dose and recheck anti-HBs in 1-2 weeks (anamnestic rise supports prior immunity/resolved infection).

questions.question: PM Q7. Patient has serology of HBsAg (-), HBcAb (+), HBsAb (-).

parts.text: a) What are 4 possible explanations?
b) If repeat is positive, what are two ways you could work this up further?

cohort_answer.text:
Remote resolved infection; Recovering from acute infection; False positive (i.e. susceptible); Occult hepatitis B (low level chronic infection); Recent IVIG
Test for HBV DNA; IgM/G fraction HBcAb. Presence of anti-HBsAb and anti-HBcAb (IgG) indicates recovery and immunity, whereas successful vaccination produces antibody only to HBsAg. Give a dose of vaccine - if HBsAb positive after vaccination then not chronic infection; consider repeating in 2-4 weeks

questions.question: Pregnant mom without prenatal care delivered baby. She's found to have HIV and HBV.

parts.text: What are two methods to prevent HIV transmission to baby?
2 methods to prevent HBV transmission to baby.

cohort_answer.text: HIV prevention: Antepartum ART ASAP (tenofovir + lamivudine/FTC if HIV/HBV co-infected); intrapartum C-section at 38 weeks if unsuppressed; neonatal AZT or combination ARV if high risk; postpartum no breastfeeding, ARV (AZT, nevirapine, lamivudine) x6 weeks. HBV prevention: Passive immunization - HBV immunoglobulin within 12h of birth (up to 7 days); Active immunization - first dose of HBV vaccine series (different leg), 3 doses total; also antiviral therapy for mothers with high viral load (>200K in 3rd trimester)

questions.question: Pregnant lady at 14 weeks gestation with HBsAg positive.

parts.text: Name 1 test you would do that would influence management.
If you were to start anti-viral, what and when would you start?
What 2 things do you tell obstetrician to avoid doing during labour and delivery?

cohort_answer.text: Test: Viral Load (if >200,000 IU/mL, start antivirals in 3rd trimester; HBeAg would not change management). Antiviral: Tenofovir (TDF) preferred (Telbivudine Category B alternative); start at 28-32 weeks (AASLD/CASL) or 24-28 weeks (EASL), continue until 12 weeks post-delivery. Avoid during labour: forceps and scalp monitor or vacuum (no evidence C-section prevents infection); avoid blood/traumatic delivery

questions.question: AM 20. HBcore Ab + isolated

parts.text: a. Which 3 things could it be other than false + (1.5)
b. Repeat serology was negative, what 2 tests to do to figure it out (2)

cohort_answer.text: a) Acute infection ('window' - cAb starts ~6 weeks post exposure, sAb ~30 weeks, requires HBsAg to not be detectable which is less common); remote infection - cleared, anti-HBs dropped below detection; chronic infection - HBsAg fallen below detection; recent IVIG; HB surface antigen mutant. b) Full serology and HBsAg including IgM fraction of anti-HBc (exclude acute infection); HBV DNA.

questions.question: Isolated Hep B core Ab (they forgot to give you Hep B sAb, assume negative)

parts.text: 3 explanations excluding false + for cAb
Repeat testing is the same. What 2 procedures can you do to help sort out cause?

questions.model_answer: a) Explanations for isolated anti-HBc positive, excluding false positive (3): (1) Window period of acute HBV infection. (2) Resolved past infection with anti-HBs waned to undetectable. (3) Occult chronic HBV infection with HBsAg below assay detection limit. b) Procedures to sort out cause (2): (1) HBV DNA testing. (2) Vaccine challenge with repeat anti-HBs testing to look for anamnestic response (suggests prior immunity).

questions.question: Hepatitis B in pregnant woman.

parts.text: What therapy would you offer?
When in pregnancy would you start it?
Based on what test?

questions.model_answer: a) Therapy: tenofovir disoproxil fumarate (safe in pregnancy, category B, high potency, low resistance). b) Timing: start in late 2nd/early 3rd trimester, typically around 28-32 weeks gestation, to reduce mother-to-child transmission risk. c) Based on: maternal HBV DNA level (start antiviral if HBV DNA >200,000 IU/mL, i.e. high viral load); infant also receives HBIG plus HBV vaccine at birth.

questions.question: Infant just born one hour ago to a mother without antenatal care who was diagnosed with HIV and HBV during delivery

parts.text: Now what can be done for newborn to reduce HIV and HBV transmission (need two for each)

cohort_answer.text: HIV: No breastfeeding; Start triple therapy ZDV+NVP+3TC (ZDV 6 weeks, 3 doses NVP first week +/-3TC); HIV test at 6 weeks. HBV: Give HBIg within 12 hours of birth; give HBV vaccine now, at 1 month and 6 months

questions.question: Hepatitis B core ab + See above

parts.text: 3-reasons why?

questions.model_answer: Reasons for isolated HBcAb positivity (3): (1) Window period of acute HBV infection (HBsAg cleared, anti-HBs not yet developed). (2) Remote resolved infection with anti-HBs having waned below detectable levels over time. (3) Occult chronic HBV infection with HBsAg below the assay's detection threshold.

questions.question: Hepatitis B serology: anti-HBSAb negative, anti-HBcAb positive, HBSAg negative

parts.text: List 4 possible explanations
Name the NEXT test to differentiate between these conditions

cohort_answer.text: 4 explanations: Recovering from acute HBV infection; Prior infection and test not sensitive enough to detect very low level of anti-HBs in serum; Susceptible with a false positive anti-HBc; Chronic infection with undetectable level of HBsAg present in serum. Next test: Hep B eAg/Ab - Early antigen, present in setting of acute viral replication and infectivity, identifies cases where patient has acute HBV infection, has dropped HepBsAg but not yet seroconverted to form Hep BsAb (HepBeAg->eAb occurs prior to HepBsAg->sAb in acute infection); other groups had Hep B viral load

questions.question: With regards to hepatitis B infection. What ALT and what DNA level before you treat with AASLD (table: state ALT and HBV DNA thresholds for each scenario)

parts.text: Cirrhosis decompensated, sAg positive
HBeAg negative, no cirrhosis, asymptomatic
HBeAg positive, no cirrhosis, asymptomatic
HBsAg+, pregnant, asymptomatic. sAg positive, ALT normal

questions.model_answer: AASLD treatment thresholds (Table - Selection of Patients for Treatment in Chronic Hepatitis B): a) Decompensated cirrhosis, HBsAg positive: treat with nucleos(t)ide analogue (NUC) regardless of HBV DNA/ALT level if HBV DNA detectable; consider liver transplantation. b) HBeAg negative, no cirrhosis, asymptomatic: HBV DNA >20,000 IU/mL with ALT >2x ULN - treat with NUC (indefinite; PEG-IFN second line); if HBV DNA >2000 IU/mL with ALT 1-2x ULN - consider liver biopsy/noninvasive fibrosis assessment and treat if moderate-severe inflammation/fibrosis; if HBV DNA >2000 with ALT <ULN - observe. c) HBeAg positive, no cirrhosis, asymptomatic: HBV DNA >20,000 IU/mL, ALT <2x ULN - observe (consider biopsy if age>40, family history HCC, HIV+); if ALT >2x ULN - observe 3-6 months for spontaneous seroconversion, then treat with PEG-IFN (48 weeks) or NUC if not seroconverted. d) HBsAg positive, pregnant, asymptomatic, ALT normal: treat with tenofovir in 3rd trimester if HBV DNA >200,000 IU/mL to prevent mother-to-child transmission, regardless of ALT/AASLD chronic hepatitis criteria.

questions.question: HBsAg positive in new dialysis patient.

parts.text: What are three measures to reduce transmission, not including routine precautions, screening or immunization?

questions.model_answer: Measures to reduce HBV transmission in dialysis unit (3, excluding routine precautions/screening/immunization): (1) Dedicated dialysis machine/station used exclusively for HBsAg-positive patients (not shared or rotated). (2) Dialyze HBsAg-positive patients in a separate, physically isolated room/area from HBV-negative patients. (3) Use dedicated, non-shared equipment/supplies (e.g. trays, instruments) for that patient, not carried between stations.

questions.question: Q73 2023 Day 1. HBV treatment thresholds (ALT and HepB DNA). (VIRUSES)

parts.text: Decompensated or compensated cirrhosis (not sure which)
eAg+, no symptoms, no cirrhosis
eAg-, no symptoms, no cirrhosis
Pregnant (just wants HepB level, no liver enzymes)

cohort_answer.text:
Cirrhosis: All patients with cirrhosis and detectable HBV DNA levels should be treated.
eAg+, no symptoms, no cirrhosis: HBeAg-positive patients (and HBeAg negative patients) in whom HBV DNA is ≥2000 IU/mL with elevated ALT (>1 ULN) for 6 months should be considered for treatment.
eAg-, no symptoms, no cirrhosis: Same threshold as above - HBV DNA ≥2000 IU/mL with elevated ALT (>1 ULN) for 6 months should be considered for treatment.
Pregnant: HBV DNA >200,000 should initiate treatment at 24-32 weeks to reduce risk of vertical transmission; TDF can be stopped at delivery or up to 12 weeks postpartum if used to prevent vertical transmission.

questions.question: Q83 2023 Day 2. HepBsAg positive dialysis patient. (VIRUSES)

parts.text: 3 things you can do aside from immunization and standard IPC precautions

cohort_answer.text: Separate room or dialysis area; dedicated dialysis machines and equipment; dedicated staff member not caring for susceptible patients at the same time; do not reuse or reprocess dialyzers.
cohort_answer.source: H-exams 2024 (answer slide (CDC recommendations for chronic hemodialysis patients))

questions.question: Your patient was unfortunately just diagnosed with autoimmune hepatitis and will need to start Rituximab very soon. Preceding blood work is as follows: HBV core antibody POSITIVE, HBV surface antibody POSITIVE, HBV surface antigen NEGATIVE, HBV DNA NEGATIVE.

parts.text: Please explain this serology result?
What TWO management considerations that are important in this case?

questions.model_answer: a) Serology (anti-HBc+, anti-HBs+, HBsAg-, HBV DNA undetectable) represents resolved past HBV infection with immunity. b) Two management considerations before rituximab: (1) Risk of HBV reactivation with B-cell-depleting therapy (rituximab) even in resolved infection with isolated/combined core+surface antibody pattern - high-risk scenario requiring antiviral prophylaxis (e.g. entecavir or tenofovir) for the duration of rituximab therapy and for 6-12 months after completion. (2) Regular monitoring of HBV DNA and LFTs during and after treatment to detect reactivation early.
questions.beyond_mandell: AASLD/ASCO hepatitis B reactivation prophylaxis guidance for immunosuppressive therapy

questions.question: Psych patient with HIV/HBV is admitted. His Atripla is stopped by Psych.

parts.text: What are 2 adverse effects that could happen?

cohort_answer.text: Can lead to HBV flare in 1/3 of patients and possible decompensation of liver disease; Development of HIV resistance

questions.question: HIV + patient co-infected with Hepatitis B. Doing well on ARVs in terms of CD4 and VL but LFTs are increasing as is the Hep B viral load. In addition, he has very high lipids that have not responded to diet and exercise.

parts.text: How would you change his therapy, justify your decision?

cohort_answer.text: If on lamivudine monotherapy: TDF or TAF should be added; avoid others like emtricitabine (cross resistance to lamivudine) or entecavir (partial cross-resistance if lamivudine resistance+). If on tenofovir or entecavir: check adherence, resistance profile, drug interactions (no known tenofovir resistance mutations). For cirrhotic patients, add a second agent (e.g. entecavir to tenofovir). Avoid PIs – high risk for increased lipids, CV risk. Also avoid ABC – high risk CV

questions.question: Woman with no antenatal care presents in labor, tests positive for HIV and Hepatitis B on rapid testing.

parts.text: 2 strategies to decrease risk of HBV transmission to baby

cohort_answer.text: IV zidovudine during labor until delivery; Elective CS recommended before rupture of membranes if VL unknown; Measure mom's VL and resistance testing; Avoid breastfeeding; Avoid fetal scalp monitoring

questions.question: Hepatitis B in pregnancy at 14 weeks

parts.text: What is the treatment?
What test?
When to start
What treatments in baby with timing?
Does the baby need follow up?
Safe to breastfeed?

cohort_answer.text: A) TDF is preferred: "Because it has extensive safety data and a lack of resistance in HBV, TDF is the preferred NA for pregnant women and those with child-bearing potential." B) HBsAg in the first trimester. Those documented to be HBsAg positive require subsequent testing for HBeAg, anti-Hbe, HBV DNA quantification, ALT to assess their stage of disease. C) Typically start at 24-32 weeks to prevent MTCT transmission; start earlier if risk factors for preterm labor, multiple gestations, planned invasive procedures (amnio); start in 2nd trimester if high viral load (>10^9). Pregnant women with HBV DNA of more than 200,000 IU/mL should initiate antiviral therapy at 24-32 weeks (~28 weeks) of gestation to reduce the risk of vertical transmission; may stop at delivery or up to 12 weeks postpartum if given strictly to prevent MTCT. D) Baby should receive HBIg and HBV vaccine within 12h of birth (with second and third doses of vaccine at 1 and 6 months). E) Yes - follow up vaccine dose 2 and 3 at 1 and 6 months respectively. Babies should be tested for HBsAg and anti-HBs between 1 and 4 months after the last dose of vaccine to confirm that they are uninfected and immune. Check Baby's sAg and sAb; if positive, baby is infected with HBV. If negative but not immune, vaccinate again with 2 additional doses until sAb >10 (immune). F) Yes as long as mom's nipples aren't cracking. Hep B is found in breastmilk but even pre-vaccine era was not associated with transmission. C section not recommended, no effect on MTCT.

questions.question: Woman with no antenatal care presents in labor, tests + for HIV and HBV on rapid testing

parts.text: 2 strategies to decrease the risk of HIV transmission to baby
2 strategies to decrease risk of HBV transmission to baby?

cohort_answer.text: A) Start ART asap; IV ZDV during labor and until delivery if VL>1000; avoid invasive procedures; consider CS if VL>1000; start PEP for baby (ZDV+NVP+3TC x6 weeks); avoid breastfeeding. B) Maternal antiviral tx; HBIg at birth (within 12h); HepB vaccine at birth (within 12h) followed by dose 2 and 3 at 1 and 6 months respectively.

questions.question:
Q10 (2013 AM)
HBV cAb + only

parts.text: A) Three explanations other than false positives
B) What two tests of interventions will help you sort is out?

cohort_answer.text:
A: 1. Recovering from acute HBV infection 2. Prior infection and test not sensitive enough to detect very low level of anti-HBs in serum 3. Susceptible with a false positive anti-HBc 4. Chronic infection with undetectable level of HBsAg present in the serum. *so either the HepB cAb is false positive, one of the other tests is a false negative. Hep BsAg either too low to detect from chronic infection or window period where it has dropped but sAb has not yet formed. Hep B eAg/Ab: Early antigen, present in setting of acute viral replication and infectivity so will identify cases where patient has acute HBV infection, has dropped HepBsAg but not yet seroconverted to form Hep B sAb. Hep BeAg-> eAb occurs prior to HepBsAg -> sAb in acute infection

B: HBeAb/Ag - Repeat HBsAb, HBsAg, HBcAb with IgM fraction, reasonable if worried about acute infection. DNA level

questions.question:
Q15 (2008)
Man travel to asia who had unprotected sex but recalls an acute hepatitis like picture 4 months ago, Returns with normal LFTs but with HepBSAg +ve. EAg+ve, E Ab -ve and DNA 20,000.

parts.text: A. What do you do?
B. Returns in six months with increased LFTs EAg -ve and E Ab +ve and DNA 5000. What to do?
C. He is interested in IFN - one advantage?

cohort_answer.text:
A: If ALT normal, and non-invasive fibrosis assessment (transient elastography) is negative, would monitor for q3 months

B: If ALT (>1x upper limit of normal) remains elevated for 6 months or hepatic fibrosis present, should undergo hepatitis B treatment

C: Advantages | Disadvantages - Finite-duration therapy; No concern with respect to viral resistance | systemic side effects; route of administration (subcutaneous injection)

questions.question:
Q16 (2007)
Man on dialysis who's brother is a prospective kidney donor but is anti-HBc positive

parts.text: A. Two possible explanations
B. The nephrologists wants to use the donor kidney.  Explain risks and counsel.

cohort_answer.text:
A: False negative sAg e.g. from mutation (e.g. chronic infection). HBsAg fallen to below cutoff of detection in chronic HBV i.e. occult HBV. 'Natural immunity' e.g. cleared infection with HBV latency, anti-HBS has fallen to zero e.g. acute infection remote, never sAg positive. Window period during acute infection (predominantly IgM class). Maternal Ab transmission to newborn

B: HBV causes high morbidity in renal transplantation as viral replication more persistent and more challenging to seroconvert sAg if infected. Risks depend on whether or not recipient is sAb positive, and whether this persists post transplant. Overall risk of 0-5.2% quoted, with risk negligible if recipient immune. No prophylaxis needed if HBV immune recipient receives from anti-HBc positive donor. If non immune, can check donor DNA level. If negative, no prophylaxis needed. If positive, can give antiviral or HBIG prophylaxis for 6-12 mo. Should check liver enzymes, sAg and HBV DNA Q3mo for 12 mo, and then Q6mo indefinitely if sAg positive donor. From an infection control perspective, treat these recipients as if they have HBV e.g. counsel on sharing household items that can be contaminated with blood.
British transplant society: The HBcAb positive (HBsAg negative) donor liver can be used for any potential liver recipient. (1C) When the liver comes from a HBcAb positive donor and is given to a HBV immune or non-immune recipient, prophylactic lamivudine should be given from the time of transplantation, and should be continued indefinitely. (1A)

questions.question:
Q17 (2006 PM)
Patient from Asia with chronic hepatitis B and elevated LFTs (3-5 times normal)

parts.text: A. What investigations are necessary before starting treatment
B. What therapies are possible (2)

cohort_answer.text:
A: Assess liver disease: Hepatic panel (ALT/AST/bili/GGT), platelets, INR, albumin. Assess HBV replication: HBeAg/anti-HBe, HBV DNA (could be determining factor regarding treatment). Assess for viral coinfections: serology for HIV, HepA, HepC, HepD (in persons from HepD endemic countries and IVDU); give HepA vaccine if unimmunized. Screen for HCC: AFP + US. Consider liver biopsy to grade and stage liver disease (not often done)

B: Pegylated Interferon alpha (pegIFNa) - generally only if HBeAg positive. Nucleo(s)tide inhibitors: Entecavir, Tenofovir, (Lamivudine, Adefovir, telbivudine)

questions.question:
Q18 (2006 PM)
HCW with previous hepatitis vaccine in the past and was never checked for positive titres,  now has negative serology

parts.text: A. Two possible explanations for this
B. What further investigations would you do?

cohort_answer.text:
A: Waning immunity. Vaccine non-responder (< 10% with standard 3 dose series)

B: Repeat HBsAb, HBsAg, HBcAb and obtain liver enzymes. If all negative (i.e. anti-HBs < 10), would complete second series of 3 vaccines and test for seroconversion 1-2 months after completion of series. There is some evidence that non-responders exhibit a better response when HBV/HAV vaccine given e.g. Twinrix. JID 2008 PMID 18544037. If KNOWN to have responded previously, but then lost sAb and at risk (e.g. IHD), can consider single booster dose of vaccine - may also benefit from higher dose. Non-responders include advanced age, smoking/higher BMI, chronic disease like CKD and other immunosuppression, celiac disease, genetic HLA variants

questions.question: HBV in pregnancy at 14 weeks.

parts.text: What non-serological test will help you determine if treatment is warranted.
What treatment.
When should it be started.
HBV table with every drug possible and must name one test required to follow adverse effects.

cohort_answer.text: Non-serological test: Hep B DNA/viral load; ALT. Treatment: First line: tenofovir; Second line: telbivudine or lamivudine; then monitor ALT every 3-6 months following discontinuation of antivirals, if normal and no active disease, just follow up clinically. When started: If HepBeAg negative - for prevention of mother-child transmission, start in 3rd trimester (28-32wks GA) with VL >200,000 regardless of eAg/ALT, can d/c at delivery (only if reason for starting is VL>200,000 and asymptomatic) or 4 weeks post partum; if HBeAg positive, treat same as non-pregnant females. Drug/monitoring table: TDF - Cr and bone density; Entecavir - LFTs; 3TC - lactic acidosis, CBC; Telbivudine - CPK (low barrier to resistance, good for pregnancy); Interferon gamma - TSH (hypothyroid)

questions.question: Table of antivirals for HBV treatment. Name one laboratory test to monitor for each: Adefovir, Tenofovir, Entecavir, Lamivudine, Telbivudine, PEG-INF

parts.text: Name side effects and monitoring test for each drug

cohort_answer.text: Adefovir: SE lactic acidosis/hepatic steatosis, renal exacerbation, hematuria; monitor ALT, Cr, PO4, lactate/CO2, U/A (avoid in HIV+). Tenofovir: SE osteomalacia/Fanconi syndrome; monitor electrolytes/PO4, CrCl. Entecavir: SE lactic acidosis, alopecia; monitor lactate/CO2, kidney function. Lamivudine: SE lactic acidosis/hepatic steatosis, pancreatitis, neutropenia, rhabdomyolysis; monitor ALT, AST, CO2/lactate, CBC, CK. Telbivudine: SE myalgias, steatosis, lactic acidosis; monitor CK, CO2, ALT/AST. PEG-INF: SE elevated ALP/ALT, neutropenia, thrombocytopenia, hypothyroidism; monitor CBC, TSH, LFT

parts.text: Name 6 different viruses that cause cancer and what type of cancer?

questions.model_answer: (1) Human papillomavirus (HPV) - cervical, anal, vulvar/vaginal/penile, and oropharyngeal squamous cell carcinoma. (2) Hepatitis B virus - hepatocellular carcinoma. (3) Hepatitis C virus - hepatocellular carcinoma. (4) Epstein-Barr virus - Burkitt lymphoma, nasopharyngeal carcinoma, Hodgkin lymphoma. (5) Human herpesvirus-8 (HHV-8/KSHV) - Kaposi sarcoma, primary effusion lymphoma, multicentric Castleman disease. (6) Human T-lymphotropic virus type 1 (HTLV-1) - adult T-cell leukemia/lymphoma (Merkel cell polyomavirus causing Merkel cell carcinoma is another acceptable answer).

questions.question: Viral table

parts.text: Complete the table (Nucleic Acid, Envelope, Antiviral) for: Mumps, Measles, Hepatitis B, EBV, Ebola, Zika

questions.model_answer: Mumps: single-stranded negative-sense RNA, enveloped; no specific antiviral (supportive care only). Measles: single-stranded negative-sense RNA, enveloped; no specific antiviral (supportive care; ribavirin has been used off-label in severe cases). Hepatitis B: partially double-stranded DNA, enveloped; antivirals - tenofovir, entecavir (also lamivudine/adefovir/telbivudine). EBV: double-stranded DNA, enveloped; no specific approved antiviral for routine infection (ganciclovir/valganciclovir used off-label for select EBV-driven disease). Ebola virus: single-stranded negative-sense RNA, enveloped; antivirals - monoclonal antibody cocktails (e.g., REGN-EB3/inmazeb, ansuvimab) and remdesivir has been studied. Zika virus: single-stranded positive-sense RNA, enveloped; no approved antiviral (supportive care only).
